title: Building digital capability for inclusive higher education: a scoping review of staff development and unequal digital capital
text_snippet: Building digital capability for inclusive higher education: a scoping review of staff development and unequal digital capital Digital literacy and digital capability have become institutional necessities in higher education rather than desirable add-ons, particularly in universities with increasingly diverse student cohorts. In these contexts, equitable participation is shaped not only by students’ access to devices and connectivity, but also by the digital capability of academic staff and the extent to which institutions enable staff to develop effective digital teaching practices. Using Bourdieu’s concept of capital as a framing lens, this scoping review examines how inequalities in staff digital competence and professional development contribute to uneven distributions of digital capital and influence inclusive learning opportunities. The review was conducted in line with established scoping review guidance, with searches across multiple databases, supported by grey literature retrieval and citation chasing. Studies were screened against predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, with selection reported through a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram. title: Widening access for lifelong learners: a case study of higher education pathway leaders in college-based higher education using activity theory
text_snippet: Widening access for lifelong learners: a case study of higher education pathway leaders in college-based higher education using activity theory This case study explores the activity systems relating to the practice of ‘widening access’ opportunities for lifelong learners to undergraduate higher education (HE) study, from the perspective of HE pathway leaders in college-based higher education (CBHE). This demographic of professional represents a subsection of the main subject stakeholders operating within a stratified HE system and widening participation (WP) agenda, responsible for the operational, managerial and day to day functioning of activities centred around the objective of widening access. Grounded in cultural-historical activity theory, the research investigates the contradictions HE pathway leaders encounter using a qualitative case study approach. Data was gathered through semi-structured interviews with pathway leaders, allowing for an in-depth analysis of tensions across key elements of the activity systems. Findings reveal that pathway leaders often employ innovative, vocationally aligned strategies, condensed timetables and technology-enhanced study modalities to overcome structural rigidity and support lifelong learners. title: Support for students with mental health conditions in UK Higher Education: the role and impact of Mental Health Advisers
text_snippet: Support for students with mental health conditions in UK Higher Education: the role and impact of Mental Health Advisers The past 25 years have witnessed a rise in Higher Education (HE) students and applicants disclosing mental health conditions, leading to the establishment of support roles, including the Mental Health Adviser (MHA). This study investigates the development, growth, and impact of MHAs within UK HE, drawing on a comprehensive literature review and focus groups. The positive outcomes of MHA support include the achievement of students’ personal goals and broader institutional objectives like completion and progression. Assessing, managing and holding risk is a key component of the MHA role leading to increased student safety and stability. Recommendations call for future research and evaluation to adopt a co-production approach with MHAs and students to refine the metrics used for evidencing the role’s contribution. Content note: this article includes brief mentions of suicide and self-harm.

title: Unravelling the impact of the ‘Be Positive’ pilot programme at CQUniversity: exploring educator perspectives on Enabling students’ personal growth and well-being
text_snippet: Unravelling the impact of the ‘Be Positive’ pilot programme at CQUniversity: exploring educator perspectives on Enabling students’ personal growth and well-being Many institutions are seeking to integrate programmes that positively impact the overall well-being and mindset of students in the higher education (HE) setting. To investigate the impact of positive psychology (PP) in improving student well-being, a PP programme, termed the ‘Be Positive’ programme, was implemented in regional Queensland in early 2023. It involved a group of Enabling students (i.e. individuals who are enrolled in a pre-bachelor foundation course designed to help them gain the skills, knowledge and confidence needed for HE). The current study sought to understand the educators’ perspectives on the programme’s impact, aiming to identify their experiences of delivering the programme as well as their perceptions of the impact on students. The findings revealed that educators perceived a range of wellness benefits for students, while also identifying certain barriers to the programme’s effectiveness.

title: Beyond the first hurdle: experiences of widening participation students at a London medical school
text_snippet: Beyond the first hurdle: experiences of widening participation students at a London medical school Expanding access to medical education for students from under-represented backgrounds has long been a key policy objective in the UK Government to promote social mobility. Efforts to improve equity in medical school admissions have included contextualised offers and targeted widening participation (WP) initiatives. However, limited research exists on the experiences and progress of students from WP backgrounds once they enter medical school. This exploratory, qualitative study explores the experiences of students from WP backgrounds at University College London Medical School to identify barriers and opportunities for support, ensuring equitable progression. The chosen methodology was a qualitative explorative case-study approach. Eligible students were recruited via email and online platforms based on self-identification. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, and transcripts were analysed to identify emerging themes. Five key themes emerged: (1) financial barriers, (2) cultural and social adjustment, (3) access to support systems and resources, (4) navigating university life, and (5) future aspirations and identity. title: Where do they come from? Why are they here? Understanding equity students’ access to higher education through a Bourdieusian lens
text_snippet: Where do they come from? Why are they here? Understanding equity students’ access to higher education through a Bourdieusian lens Enabling programmes in Australia play a crucial role in addressing inequities in higher education (HE) by providing targeted support to students from underrepresented backgrounds. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theoretical concepts of habitus, cultural capital, social capital and field, this study examines how these factors shape the experiences of equity students as they enter HE through an Enabling programme. Using a case study methodology, the research explores the narratives of students enrolled in an Australian Enabling programme, highlighting their aspirations and the barriers they encounter. Findings reveal that students often face systemic disadvantages, including disrupted educational trajectories, socio-economic hardships, and limited access to academic resources. However, Enabling programmes act as transformative spaces that foster self-efficacy, social mobility and academic preparedness. Through tailored support and the cultivation of ‘determined hope’, students navigate and reconfigure their habitus to succeed within the university field. The study underscores the necessity of recognising and addressing disparities in cultural and social capital to ensure equitable access and s

title: Broadening access to global learning: the transformative potential of virtual mobility
text_snippet: Broadening access to global learning: the transformative potential of virtual mobility This article explores the transformative potential of virtual mobility in widening participation in global learning within higher education. Traditionally centred on physical travel, academic mobility has long excluded students facing financial, caregiving, legal and disability-related barriers. Virtual mobility (defined as cross-border academic engagement via digital technologies) offers a scalable and more equitable alternative. Drawing on examples such an international week embedded in an MA programme, the authors illustrate how virtual formats can foster inclusion, build intercultural competence, and enhance employability through structured and collaborative experiences. However, the paper also highlights persistent challenges, including digital inequities, engagement issues and the limited immersive quality of online interactions. To unlock virtual mobility’s full potential, institutions must embed it into curricula, provide digital access support and employ intentional pedagogical design. The authors argue for a reimagined model of internationalisation, one that prioritises equity, flexibility and real-world relevance in an increasingly digital and interconnected world.

title: Engaging boys in higher education outreach: learning from practice
text_snippet: Engaging boys in higher education outreach: learning from practice Differences in higher education (HE) participation by gender are a significant topic of discussion worldwide. Addressing these disparities requires targeted initiatives to promote equality in HE. This paper draws on case study research involving ten projects designed to engage boys in outreach in England, where HE participation of boys continues to lag behind other groups. This article illustrates different approaches to delivering outreach with boys and highlights common themes and the most promising approaches to working with boys, including activities for working-class boys who are the most underrepresented group. This paper proposes some reflective questions for practitioners when developing outreach activities with the target group of working-class boys and makes recommendations for practice. It will support outreach providers when thinking about the design, delivery and evaluation of new models of HE outreach which have the best potential to engage boys and support their onward progression in education.

title: Relational mentoring in postgraduate research: Black scholars’ experiences of the ASPIRE programme
text_snippet: Relational mentoring in postgraduate research: Black scholars’ experiences of the ASPIRE programme Black students’ under-representation in postgraduate research (PGR) pathways within the UK higher education (HE) sector reflects persistent structural inequalities rather than episodic participation gaps. While widening participation scholarship has focused largely on undergraduate access, less attention has been paid to relational and epistemic barriers shaping doctoral trajectories. Grounded in critical race theory and anti-deficit scholarship, this article examines how Black scholars participating in a culturally grounded mentoring programme interpreted their experiences within racialised PGR contexts. Drawing on qualitative data from semi-structured interviews and dialogic ‘listening rooms’, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and a multistakeholder round-table analysis, the study integrates Bell’s (2018) concept of the permanence of racism, Delgado’s (1989) counter-storytelling, and Yosso’s (2005) community cultural wealth framework alongside Ubuntu (Tutu, 1999) and Omoluabi (Oyeshile, 2021) philosophies. Findings indicate that participants described identity affirmation, bounded belonging and strengthened navigational agency. Rather than framing these shifts as remed

title: Expanding horizons: the role of ethics of care in a widening participation programme for first-generation students
text_snippet: Expanding horizons: the role of ethics of care in a widening participation programme for first-generation students This article explores a widening participation programme for adolescents, aged 12‐16, living in territorially stigmatised communities. The study focuses on a programme component in which university student ambassadors offer homework support. Drawing on Noddings’ ethics of care, Biesta’s concept of subjectification, and Bourdieu’s theory of social reproduction, the study examines how such programmes can foster motivation, self-efficacy, and well-being beyond simply increasing interest in higher education, while identifying challenges in sustaining motivation for continued studies. Based on field observations, interviews and focus groups, the analysis highlights that caring relationships, role models and locally anchored practices can play a central role in creating supportive spaces where students feel seen, safe and encouraged to engage academically. The findings also indicate that for encounters to develop into meaningful connections, both time and sustained engagement are essential. Student ambassadors play a crucial role in fostering trust-based interactions and opportunities for identification, which can strengthen aspirations and empower students. title: Supporting forced-migrants’ pathways to and through university: what were the aims, processes and outcomes of a collaboration between a university and their local government authority?
text_snippet: Supporting forced-migrants’ pathways to and through university: what were the aims, processes and outcomes of a collaboration between a university and their local government authority? This article charts the origins, beginnings, processes and outcomes of a project to offer appropriate language training to forced-migrants whose access to higher education had been interrupted. Qualifying individuals were offered the chance to progress with the relevant language training to a level appropriate for higher education, and on the basis that after completion they would be applying to study at a UK university. It outlines the challenges involved, the impact the project had on all participants and what was learned in the process. It also highlights the development of a founding relationship between a university and its local government authority, to deliver this initiative and carry it forward, and explains how it was achieved.

title: Operationalising evaluation of attainment raising interventions within widening participation: a case study evaluating a literacy intervention
text_snippet: Operationalising evaluation of attainment raising interventions within widening participation: a case study evaluating a literacy intervention This study investigates a reading support programme, offering key insights into the challenges of evaluating attainment-raising programmes within widening participation contexts in England. The research identifies three primary challenges: resource and infrastructure limitations, stakeholder engagement complexities, and data reliability, which present challenges to implementation and evaluation of such interventions. The findings highlight the limitations of rigid, standardised evaluation frameworks, arguing that these approaches often fail to capture the full impact of interventions targeting disadvantaged student populations. Instead, this study advocates for a phronetic approach that emphasises practitioner-based, context-sensitive knowledge. By integrating experiential insights from practitioners, the research presents an adaptive evaluation strategy that better reflects the realities of educational environments.

title: Similar student support in very different places: the impacts of undergraduate bursaries in two Russell Group universities
text_snippet: Similar student support in very different places: the impacts of undergraduate bursaries in two Russell Group universities Bursaries are an integral component of WP strategies within UK Higher Education. Therefore, it is imperative that they succeed in accomplishing their goal; even more so at a time where UK students are increasingly struggling financially. While the (light) evidence suggests bursaries can help students from lower-income families ‘get on’ at university in the same way as their more affluent peers, there is a lack of research on how ‘place’ affects bursary effectiveness; this study aims to fill that gap. We compare student survey data and education and employment outcomes using two very different Russell Group universities as case studies to better understand how bursary delivery context affects the bursary’s effectiveness. While bursaries provided a substitute for earned income or family resources in both universities, our analysis also showed that bursary holders differed significantly from non-holders in only one of the two case study universities in other areas, such as perceptions of financial position and post-university outcomes. The findings show that bursaries work, albeit to different extents in different places, confirming a spatial element to bursary provision. The characte

title: Can success on a foundation science course be attributed to factors such as entry qualifications, ethnicity, gender or widening participation?
text_snippet: Can success on a foundation science course be attributed to factors such as entry qualifications, ethnicity, gender or widening participation? The Science with a Foundation Year (SFY) programme at the University of Nottingham (UoN) provides students, who don't have the correct direct entry requirements, with the opportunity to gain the equivalent skills and knowledge required for progression on to a variety of science degrees. This study investigates the academic outcomes of students enrolled in the SFY programme at the University of Nottingham, focusing on the influence of entry qualifications, ethnicity (identified as global majority or not), gender, and widening participation (WP) status. Drawing on institutional data from 2017‐2024, the analysis reveals that students with more applied, vocational qualifications (BTEC) ‐ particularly males from global majority (GM) and WP backgrounds ‐ exhibit lower pass and progression rates compared to their peers studying the more academic Level 3 qualifications (A-Levels). However, BTEC female students, especially those meeting WP criteria, demonstrate more favourable outcomes. The journal article critically examines these disparities through the lens of equity and access, questioning the adequacy of traditional sector success metrics, such as student achievement of 'good degrees'

title: ‘We should be fuelling their passion’: A phenomenological exploration of the role of teachers in careers guidance for students applying to medical school from widening participation backgrounds
text_snippet: ‘We should be fuelling their passion’: A phenomenological exploration of the role of teachers in careers guidance for students applying to medical school from widening participation backgrounds Widening participation remains a key priority for medical schools, but to date, progress has been limited. Previous work has identified that a significant barrier to universities achieving more substantial change is that a limited number of students from deprived backgrounds apply to medical schools. Increasingly, evidence has shown that secondary schools play an essential and under-researched role. Semi-structured interviews were undertaken with science teachers working in schools with higher-than-average levels of socio-economic deprivation. These were analysed with a descriptive phenomenological methodology using a Bourdieusian theoretical framework. Teachers described providing social capital to students from underrepresented backgrounds, thereby helping them to overcome inequalities. The teachers work in a broader system; their role being shaped by the institutional habitus of the school in which they work. They also identified several barriers to their role, including highlighting inadequate time or money available to allow them to carry out the role and a lack of training for it. title: Access practitioners in Irish Higher Education: a national mixed-methods study of role, identity and vision
text_snippet: Access practitioners in Irish Higher Education: a national mixed-methods study of role, identity and vision Access practitioners are central to widening participation and inclusion in Irish higher education, yet their work remains under-examined. This article presents findings from a national mixed-methods study comprising a survey ( n =121) and three World Cafés with practitioners ( n =54) across fourteen Higher Education Institutions (HEIs). Access practitioners are primarily motivated by social justice commitments and lived experience, and describe a relational, agile practice that spans outreach, student support, advocacy and institutional change. Key challenges include short-term and inflexible funding, administrative burden, ‘role creep and limited formal recognition. Research participants report increasing complexity of student need and emotional labour with risks of burnout. Research participants articulate a future that embeds a whole-of-institution approach to access, sustained funding and supervision structures, and formal professional development and recognition including a professional body and accredited training. title: Words matter: the language of widening participation
text_snippet: Words matter: the language of widening participation This discussion article draws on the authors’ extensive experience to reflect on the impact of the language of widening participation on learners, practitioners and researchers in higher education. Noting different but related terms are used in the UK and Australia, the historic development of the phrase ‘widening participation’ and its reductive acronym ‘WP’ in policy is explored and problematised. Recommendations are made for the sector to critique the taken‐for‐granted use of the ‘widening participation’ phrase for greater inclusivity.

title: Inclusion and inclusivity: a reflective critical discussion
text_snippet: Inclusion and inclusivity: a reflective critical discussion Words matter, and the use of the word ‘inclusion’ is no exception. The words ‘inclusion’, ‘inclusivity’ and ‘inclusive’ have seen increasing prominence in widening participation, and yet it is not always clear that we are all talking about the same concept or working towards a common goal. Moreover, I argue the concept of inclusion is often paired with equality/equity and/or diversity without critical evaluation of whether this is appropriate. Increasingly, these semantic tensions play out in universities’ efforts towards building an ‘inclusive curriculum’. Uncritical use of that term risks unwisely conflating a rich variety of approaches and being appropriated towards ends that run counter to equity and justice for marginalised students. As universities move towards implementation of inclusion, I use the metaphor of an ‘inclusivity machine’ to illustrate the problems with viewing inclusion as a process to be operationalised within the neoliberal university. I conclude with a reflection on whether inclusion is the goal to which universities and practitioners should aspire. This discussion piece will critically reflect on uses of the word ‘inclusion’, drawing from personal experienc

title: Beyond labels: the complexities of defining non-traditional students in higher education
text_snippet: Beyond labels: the complexities of defining non-traditional students in higher education This article is based on a systematic literature review of 196 publications, aimed at analysing global definitions of ‘non-traditional’ students (NTS) and their broader implications. NTS are often identified by characteristics such as age, educational background, or non-standard access pathways to higher education, but the lack of a unified definition creates ambiguity. In some contexts, these categorisations rely on comparisons to a presumed ‘standard’ student profile, which no longer reflects the diversity of today’s student populations. This article examines how language constructs binary distinctions between traditional and non-traditional students, often reinforcing exclusionary norms while also offering potential for reimagining inclusive identities. By incorporating an intersectional perspective, the article highlights how overlapping social categories such as gender, ethnicity and socioeconomic status shape unique challenges for NTS. This complexity underscores the inadequacy of rigid definitions and the need to address structural barriers that impact student access and success. title: Neurodivergent, neurodiverse, autistic and ADHD ‐ does language impact how students engage with learning?
text_snippet: Neurodivergent, neurodiverse, autistic and ADHD ‐ does language impact how students engage with learning? Widening participation and engaging students with learning involves removing barriers, increasing inclusion and welcoming a diverse student population. Growing numbers of neurodiverse students are progressing onto higher education with or without a formal diagnosis. Academic colleagues may not have specific knowledge of the range of neurodiversity. The language we use when welcoming, supporting and engaging with our students needs to be carefully considered so that we do not exclude or put students off before they have the chance to fulfil their potential. This article explores some of the existing knowledge and provides insight from experiences facilitating online peer support skills development workshops for the neurodiverse community within a UK university.

title: Of taboos and placeholders: on the relevance of the term ‘disability’ in German institutions of higher education and higher education policy discourse
text_snippet: Of taboos and placeholders: on the relevance of the term ‘disability’ in German institutions of higher education and higher education policy discourse The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) was ratified by Germany in 2009. In the same year the German Rectors’ Conference published the statement ‘A University for All, which proclaims the expansion of supportive measures for students with disabilities in order to enhance access and participation. Now, 16 years later, German institutions of higher education are still far from having achieved ‘full inclusion’. On the contrary ‐ in their observations on the status of the implementation of the CRPD in Germany the UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities expressed its concern that in the German education system inclusion had been implemented so poorly (UN, 2023: 12). Lately, the authors have observed an increase in difficulties and uncertainties in university discourses to address or name disability. Assuming that language is an important part of forming attitudes and perceptions, this article will discuss the question whether this uncertainty can be derived from the literally ‘unspeakable’ horrors of German history concerning persons with disabilities and through the special structure of the German educational system. It will further ask how thes

title: The importance of disability‐inclusive language
text_snippet: The importance of disability‐inclusive language Disability-inclusive language has been garnering attention in recent years, and higher education providers (HEPs) need to move with the times. Outdated terminology such as ‘declare and disclose’; ‘interventions’; and ‘people with disabilities’ should be avoided to ensure disabled students and disabled staff feel welcomed, and to nurture a sense of belonging. Negative terminology perpetuates misconceptions and can contribute to discriminatory attitudes and actions. Existing and new models of disability, including the STAART Principles of Disability (SPoD) will be discussed to demonstrate the impact of language. This paper was developed from a presentation I was invited to deliver for the Open University Access, Participation and Success seminar in October 2023 and uses disability-inclusive language in a UK context.

title: The changing policy language of widening participation in the English HE market: from WP to ‘fair access’ and ‘social mobility’
text_snippet: The changing policy language of widening participation in the English HE market: from WP to ‘fair access’ and ‘social mobility’ This article analyses the changing language of ‘widening participation’, in general use since the Dearing Report of 1997 (NCIHE, 1997) and employs policy discourse analysis of six policy texts to link the evolution of language to describe the work of widening participation over almost three decades. The article shows clear links between the changing use of language of policy discourses employed to justify the ongoing marketisation of the higher education (HE) system through five stages between 1987 and 2017 (McCaig, 2018). It also explores the language changes in relation to different perspectives or lenses, most evident in the shift from the societal aim of widening participation to the individualised language of ‘social mobility’ as students came to be seen as consumers and policymakers’ attitude towards system expansion began to change, with increasing emphasis on vocational further and higher education.

title: Inclusive language and representations: an international comparison between England and Indonesia
text_snippet: Inclusive language and representations: an international comparison between England and Indonesia One of Indonesia’s Ministry of Education and Culture (MoEC) strategies is to embrace neurodiversity (ND). This paper, co-authored by academics both in England and Indonesia as part of a research project, offers an international comparison between the language and tools used to foster inclusion and widening participation in higher education (HE) for students who are neurodivergent. The umbrella terms of ‘neurodivergence’ and ‘neurodiversity’ are unpacked, along with consideration of the effects of academic understanding on student provision, engagement, retention and outcomes. Many institutions in the United Kingdom (UK) now provide disability support for ND learners at HE level, but understanding is still growing. The way we use language such as ‘acceptance’ as opposed to ‘awareness’ is key in dissolving stigma around neurodivergent conditions, and language certainly matters when inclusion can be fostered through making a shift from considering neurodiversity in light of the medical model, which sees neurodivergence through a deficit lens. We share overviews of legislation and support for people with neurodivergence in both the UK and Indonesia and consider how language and stereot

title: 'Woke', intersectionality, critical race theory and decolonisation: misunderstood, misused and weaponised
text_snippet: 'Woke', intersectionality, critical race theory and decolonisation: misunderstood, misused and weaponised The authors of this article, both educational researchers, frequently encounter misrepresentation, misunderstanding and political misuse of key terms historically used to address racial inequalities or social justice. Nationally and internationally, issues continually emerge in discussions concerning race and equity in higher education, impeding progress towards greater equity and diversity. ‘Woke’, ‘critical race theory’, ‘intersectionality’ and ‘decolonisation’ are among the terms and theories the authors have observed being weaponised, misappropriated and stripped of their original intent. While other terms have faced similar distortions, the confusion and misunderstandings of these words have resulted in their harmful and mainstream misuse against the very groups they were designed to support, hindering productive discussions and positive social justice changes. Discussions within the Network Evaluating and Researching University Participation Interventions (NERUPI) Student and Staf f Race and Ethnic Equity (SsREE) working group in the United Kingdom (UK) resulted in the production of a glossary that provides accurate definitions of frequently misused terms in race and inequali

title: Awkward associations: a critique of the language of widening participation for adult learners
text_snippet: Awkward associations: a critique of the language of widening participation for adult learners This discussion paper critically evaluates the language and terminology of widening participation within the context of adult education, especially in UK higher education. The central argument is that adult education/widening participation has always been an awkward fit in conventional educational definitions and discourse, and this is reflected in the language, which too often is insensitive to diffident prospective students. On the other hand the difficulty of finding a language for new initiatives which is free of inappropriate associations must be acknowledged. My focus will be on my own professional experience over many years in university adult/continuing education and especially those students seeking mature entry to mainstream higher education programmes.

title: On the decoding of skills and competency in the age of atomized education
text_snippet: On the decoding of skills and competency in the age of atomized education This paper critically examines the evolving landscape of knowledge, skills and competence within university continuing education units, with a focus on the increasing atomization of lifelong education into micro‐credentials and other short-cycle learning models. While these trends respond to workforce demands for skills-first employment, particularly in unregulated fields, they also raise concerns about the authenticity and coherence of educational outcomes. Drawing on insights from cognitive science, the paper explores the dynamic processes of learning, emphasising the role of mental models (schemas and world models) in integrating and applying knowledge in novel contexts. The discussion highlights the challenges posed by semantic drift and inconsistent definitions of key educational terms, which complicate the alignment of educational outcomes with labour market needs. Furthermore, it critiques the limitations of micro‐credentials in fostering the broader, adaptive competencies required to navigate complexity and uncertainty. title: Empowering change: making the case for action research for studying widening participation in undergraduate medical education
text_snippet: Empowering change: making the case for action research for studying widening participation in undergraduate medical education This paper evaluates the use of action research as a methodology to address socio-economic disparities in undergraduate medical education, which persist despite some progress in gender and ethnic representation. Traditionally, medical schools have admitted applicants with significant economic, social, and educational capital. While quantitative methods have helped track trends, they do not capture the lived experiences of marginalised groups. Action research, originating from Lewin's social intervention theory (1946), emphasises collaborative, cyclical processes involving stakeholders to create and evaluate solutions for complex social issues. Using a narrative approach, this paper reviews action research applications in education and healthcare. Although under-utilised within medical education, examples of its use are presented to illustrate its relevance to widening participation. Action research has the potential to empower underrepresented students and build community among participants, providing practical insights into the barriers and opportunities experienced. Through collaboration between students, faculty, and community members, action research can promote an inclusive cu

title: Navigating higher education assessment systems: exploring racially minoritised students’ engagement with extenuating circumstances
text_snippet: Navigating higher education assessment systems: exploring racially minoritised students’ engagement with extenuating circumstances This paper addresses an often-overlooked aspect of the student experience: extenuating circumstances (EC), a key form of support for students facing difficulties with assessments. In cases where students are unable to effectively engage with this system, they are placed at a disadvantage, which increases the risk of non-completion, particularly for widening participation students. This study investigates EC engagement among racially minoritised (RM) students within the Faculty of Arts at a large research-focused UK university. It finds that RM students apply for ECs at rates comparable to their white peers; however, disparities in engagement and perceptions of fairness remain. The paper offers the following recommendations: waive the requirement for supporting evidence; train staff in areas such as implicit bias and stereotype threat; improve data management and EC monitoring; and allocate dedicated time for support staff to assist RM students in navigating the EC process.

title: Class and belonging: preliminary results of a study into lecturer demographics in Foundation Year teaching
text_snippet: Class and belonging: preliminary results of a study into lecturer demographics in Foundation Year teaching This paper summarises ongoing research into lecturer demographics within Foundation Year (FY) teaching. It identifies the marginalised voices of working-class academics and recognises the diversity of FY students and practitioners, including those who are first-generation scholars. We explore common characteristics shared by some Foundation lecturers and consider how academics’ previous experiences impact their educational practice. Through a large-scale questionnaire and interviews, our research suggests that a significant percentage of FY practitioners are from widening participation or working-class backgrounds, and may have more in common with their students, especially in terms of experiencing inequity and having marginalised identities in their fields. Class is not a legally protected characteristic, nor a criterion for widening participation, yet anecdotally, it appears to have an impact on FY practitioners and students and their sense of belonging. This study will not only support wider understanding of FY practitioners, but improve experiences for all staff and students, helping to promote greater diversity and inclusion, and potentially influence discussions on local and

title: Leveraging the value of warm knowledge: Engaging the proximity principle through University Ambassadors in developing high-school students’ possible selves
text_snippet: Leveraging the value of warm knowledge: Engaging the proximity principle through University Ambassadors in developing high-school students’ possible selves The 2024 Australian Universities Accord sets a target of 80% of the Australian working population gaining a higher education qualification by 2050, a rise from the current attainment rate of approximately one-third of the population. The target is set against more than two decades of government investment in equity initiatives that have resulted in minimal proportional shifts of enrolment in higher education. The purpose of this current study is to investigate the role of proximity in school student’s perception of pathways to future possible selves. We draw on two consecutive years of data derived from a largescale project that placed University Ambassadors (UA) in school classrooms over a sustained period of time. Whilst findings cannot speak to participating students’ post-secondary education outcomes, our findings suggest that embedded and extended UA contact with school students facilitates the flow of warm knowledge about university experience and pathways to get there.

title: From Social Relationships to Social Support: Facilitating workshops to enhance widening participation students’ sense of belonging at medical school
text_snippet: From Social Relationships to Social Support: Facilitating workshops to enhance widening participation students’ sense of belonging at medical school Medical students from underrepresented or widening participation (WP) backgrounds often feel isolated and lack a sense of belonging in Higher Education (HE) and medical school. Frequently, they have competing demands on their time, which can result in fewer opportunities to meet peers from similar backgrounds. In a previous article, we demonstrated how workshops facilitated by staff and WP graduates helped to increase current WP medical students’ self-efficacy and sense of belonging. This paper expands on previous findings by exploring the impact of these peer relationships on participants’ Social Support. Focus groups were held with 15 participants who had attended the workshops. The focus group transcripts were iteratively coded and analysed using inductive thematic analysis. A secondary deductive analysis was then undertaken using a theoretical framework adapted from Williams et al .’s (2004) composite definition of Social Support. title: Enhancing access, participation and progression of refugee background students in English higher education
text_snippet: Enhancing access, participation and progression of refugee background students in English higher education This paper adds to the literature on refugee background students’ (RBS) access to and widening participation in Higher Education (HE) in England. It briefly outlines who may be considered as a refugee background student and then highlights changes to the governing frameworks impacting access and widening participation policy in English HE. An outline of existing literature relating to access and participation of RBS in UK HE is provided, and a gap is identified in the debate around how institutions can move beyond ‘access’ to more holistically address ‘access, participation and progression’ (OFS, 2023). A deductive thematic analysis of four English university websites is then undertaken using Wilson-Strydom’s ‘pragmatic capabilities list for transition into university’ and concepts of ‘access with success’ (2012; 2016a). Results are analysed in context to whether institutional provision enhances the capabilities of RBS to access, participate and progress in English HE, and recommendations for practice are suggested.
